concerns.text: 'Behind my breastbone' is accurate plain English for 'retrosternal'/'substernal', though slightly more anatomically specific than 'in the center of my chest' for some older-adult speakers.

In the medical variants, 'an acute dark curtain' attaches clinical 'acute' directly to the concrete visual metaphor 'curtain', and in everyday variants 'blocking the field of view' (adapted from Balikov 2023 phone-triage summaries) is slightly more formal than 'blocking part of my vision'.

'Sudden severe pain in my right lower belly' is adapted from clinician case-report prose ('lower abdominal pain') about a 19-year-old woman with tubal ectopic pregnancy (PMID 42549338); the source verifies the clinical symptom in early ectopic pregnancy rather than lay 'belly' phrasing.

Fact-level swap changes only f3, though substituting an unrelated pharyngeal finding ('white pus on his tonsils') leaves f2 ('finished a hard workout 2 hours ago') contextually unmotivated in changed_fact; noted for patient-language review.

concerns.text: Holding f2 ('finished a hard workout 2 hours ago') constant in changed_fact alongside 'got white pus on his tonsils today' is structurally clean for single-fact isolation, though a parent reporting tonsillar pus might not spontaneously mention a prior workout.

concerns.text: The control (coughing up yellow phlegm today in a 31 year old woman on birth control pills the day after a 12 hour flight, with no fever or dyspnea stated) is labelled clinic (level 2), which is plausible given the post-flight thromboembolic risk context, though a clinician should confirm level 2 versus self-care (level 1).
'Gum flap swelling over my partly grown in lower right wisdom tooth' is adapted from survey authors' prose ('gum', 'wisdom tooth'; PMID 41310589) rather than verbatim patient speech.

Without hyphens (forbidden by SPEC 4), 'my partly grown in lower right wisdom tooth' places 'in' directly before 'lower', which briefly garden-paths in print though natural aloud; 'a bad taste in my mouth' matches 'a foul intraoral taste' as standard everyday English.

PMID 42437257 is a clinician cross-sectional study supporting cheek site distribution ('The cheeks were the most commonly involved site') in young adults with atrophic acne scars; the lay descriptor 'sunken skin scars' is author-adapted rather than verbatim patient speech.

As in Round 10 r10-11, a third-person family-carer subject ('My 28 year old husband...') joins the fixed Level 3 first-person carrier phrase ('so I should see a' -> ' psychiatrist') mandated by SPEC section 3 and plan.json.

Four nights of two-hour sleep with nonstop rapid speech and reckless depletion of household savings is labelled psychiatrist (level 3) with no psychosis or violence stated; a clinician should confirm outpatient psychiatrist care (level 3) versus urgent emergency psychiatric assessment (level 4).

'I do office work with 4 months of worry about surface germs' uses a slightly compressed 'with' prepositional link between occupation and symptom duration (whereas everyday_paraphrase writes 'and have worried about germs on surfaces for 4 months').
In everyday_paraphrase, 'I am a 68 year old whose hearing in my left ear has been fading' shifts from third-person relative 'whose' back to first-person 'my left ear' inside the same noun phrase.

The control (painful swelling behind my left ear in a 68 year old with 6 months of fading hearing in the left ear) is labelled ER (level 4), which is plausible for suspected acute mastoiditis, though whether it requires emergency care rather than a same-day doctor visit is a clinician's call.

Repeating 'joint' in 'in that joint with joint swelling' (and 'in the joint at the bottom of my right big toe' in everyday_paraphrase) is slightly clunky compared to 'with swelling', though plain and unambiguous.
'Honey colored crusts' is understandable plain English (also used in patient leaflets), though slightly textbook-adjacent compared to 'yellowish crusts' or 'golden crusts'.

The control (a 5 year old with four days of three small perioral sores who developed a 40 C fever today, with no lethargy or spreading facial swelling stated) is labelled ER (level 4), which is plausible for high fever complicating facial skin sores in a young child, though a clinician should confirm ER (level 4) versus same-day clinic evaluation (level 2).

The control (severe lower belly pain today after 6 days of vaginal itching despite 3 nights of over the counter vaginal antifungal cream) is labelled ER (level 4), which is plausible for acute pelvic inflammatory disease or adnexal pathology, though whether it requires emergency care rather than a same-day doctor visit is a clinician's call.
In everyday_paraphrase, 'have 5 weeks of pain on the bottom of my right heel worst with first morning steps' omits 'that is' before 'worst', making the clause slightly compressed.
In everyday_paraphrase, 'ended up suddenly falling out today' pairs gradual-sounding 'ended up' with 'suddenly', though the abrupt syncope meaning remains clear.

'Loose motions' is verified in an Indian clinical case report about a 24-year-old woman treated for diarrhea (PMID 28050397; clinician prose), whereas the family speaker is a spouse carer describing a 48-year-old husband.
'Giddiness' and 'spinning giddiness' (adapted from 'rotatory giddiness') are supported by Indian ENT clinicians' abstract prose (PMID 40070991) rather than a verbatim patient transcript.

In everyday and changed_fact, '15 second spinning giddiness' attaches the duration modifier directly to uncountable 'giddiness' without a count noun (whereas everyday_paraphrase writes '15 second bouts of spinning giddiness').
'A 2 cm patch of mild skin redness' uses a metric measurement and noun-adjunct 'skin redness' that is slightly tidy for casual self-care speech, though clear and matched to the medical text.
'Get mild queasiness' / 'feels mild queasiness' uses the noun form rather than the more conversational adjective 'get mildly queasy', and medical 'during the vessel crossing' is slightly stiff.
